q.intro.text: A smoothie stand logged twelve summer days: each day's high temperature, and the smoothies it sold. Two of those days were eighty degrees. Tomorrow's forecast is eighty degrees. How many smoothies should the stand plan for? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the plot moves first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: Each row is one day: two numbers that belong together. Each day becomes one dot: across for the temperature, up for the smoothies. Both eighty degree days get their own dot, one above the other.

e.step1.text: Left to right, the cloud tends to go up: a positive association. The dots hug a straight edge: linear. They stay close to it: strong. A tendency, not a rule. Some hotter days sold fewer.

e.step2.text: A trend line runs through the middle of the cloud, with dots on both sides all along. It passes seventy, forty, and ninety, ninety: up fifty for twenty degrees, so the slope is two point five. Its equation is y equals two point five x, minus one hundred thirty five.

e.step3.text: Up from eighty degrees to the line, then across: about sixty five smoothies. The two real eighty degree days, fifty eight and seventy two, sit on either side. The line gives a typical day, not an exact one.

e.why.text: Quick check: why plan for about sixty five, and not seventy two?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. One day can run high or low. The line sums up all twelve.

e.why.exact.text: Look at the two real eighty degree days: fifty eight and seventy two. Days at the same temperature differ, so sixty five is an estimate.

e.why.only.text: The other ten days count too. Together they show the trend, and the trend is steadier than any one day.

t.intro.text: Same stand, same line. The first three steps are done. Now you predict for an eighty six degree day, then read what the slope and the intercept mean.

t.pred.text: Use the line, y equals two point five x, minus one hundred thirty five. About how many smoothies on an eighty six degree day?

t.pred.ok.text: Yes. Two point five times eighty six is two hundred fifteen, and minus one hundred thirty five is eighty. About eighty smoothies.

t.pred.mult.text: Two hundred fifteen is two point five times eighty six. Now take away the one hundred thirty five.

t.pred.near.text: That is a real day near eighty six degrees. The prediction comes from the line, not from one dot.

t.pred.no.text: Put eighty six in for x. Two point five times eighty six, then take away one hundred thirty five.

t.slope.text: What does the slope, two point five, mean here?

t.slope.ok.text: Yes: on average. Single days scatter around the line.

t.slope.exact.text: Look at the dots. Two days one degree apart can differ by much more, or less. The slope is an average.

t.slope.cause.text: These data show an association. Heat may well matter, but the data alone cannot prove cause.

t.int.text: The equation gives minus one hundred thirty five at zero degrees. What does that mean?

t.int.ok.text: Yes. The logged days run from sixty eight to ninety four degrees. Zero is far outside, and sales can't be negative.

t.int.real.text: No day near zero degrees was logged, and nobody sells negative smoothies. The intercept has no real meaning here.

t.int.wrong.text: The line fits the logged days well. It just should not be stretched to zero degrees.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked about sixty five, and you were right: the trend of all twelve days, not one day.

q.cb.single.text: At the start you picked seventy two, one single day. The line uses all twelve days, so it gives about sixty five.

q.cb.none.text: At the start you said you couldn't tell. The days do disagree, but the trend of all twelve still gives a fair estimate: about sixty five.

q.cb.skip.text: A trend line turns a cloud of days into a fair estimate.

p.intro.text: Riley uses the same line for a heat wave. At one hundred twenty degrees, the stand will sell one hundred sixty five smoothies. Is Riley right?

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. The dots stop at ninety four degrees, and one hundred twenty is far past them: extrapolation.

p.c2.text: Right. Past the data, nothing shows whether the pattern goes on, bends, or stops.

p.c3.text: Right. At eighty degrees the line is backed by real days on both sides. At one hundred twenty, it is not.

p.no.axis.text: How long an axis is drawn is up to whoever draws it. The dots, from sixty eight to ninety four degrees, set the range.

p.no.exact.text: No day was exactly eighty six degrees either, and eighty six is inside the range. The range matters, not exact matches.

p.no.line.text: A line on paper goes on forever. Real sales were only seen from sixty eight to ninety four degrees.

p.no.worthless.text: Too strong. Inside the logged range, the line gives fair estimates.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That's a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the plot backs every one. Riley extrapolated far past the data.
